username database"},{"cmd":"R1(config)# aaa authorization exec default local","note":"Also governs which privilege level a successful login receives, based on the local database"},{"cmd":"R1(config)# end","note":"Returns to privileged EXEC mode"},{"cmd":"R1# show running-config | include aaa","note":"Confirms the AAA configuration is active before ending the session"}],"notes":["Keeping 'local' as the authentication method (rather than only an external server not yet configured) avoids a total lockout if that external server is ever unreachable.","This backupadmin account exists specifically as a safety net separate from the netadmin account created earlier for SW1."],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: 'aaa new-model' turns on the full AAA framework, and pointing both authentication and authorization at 'local' means every login is checked and privilege-assigned from R1's own username database — a safe foundation to later extend with an external RADIUS/TACACS+ server. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: enabling 'aaa new-model' with a broken or unreachable external server as the ONLY method (no local fallback) can lock every administrator out simultaneously the moment that server becomes unreachable."},{"id":36,"title":"Branch build 36: extended ACL protecting R2's WAN edge","level":"INTER","cat":"Security","purpose":"Filter unwanted traffic at the branch's internet-facing interface.","config":["enable","configure terminal","ip access-list extended WAN-EDGE-IN","deny ip 10.10.0.0 0.0.255.255 any","permit tcp any host 203.0.113.50 eq 443","permit tcp any any established","deny ip any any log","exit","interface gigabitethernet 0/2","ip access-group WAN-EDGE-IN in","end"],"steps":[{"cmd":"R2> enable","note":"Moves from user EXEC mode into privileged EXEC mode"},{"cmd":"R2# configure terminal","note":"Moves from privileged EXEC mode into global configuration mode"},{"cmd":"R2(config)# ip access-list extended WAN-EDGE-IN","note":"Begins a named extended ACL for the branch's internet-facing side"},{"cmd":"R2(config-ext-nacl)# deny ip 10.10.0.0 0.0.255.255 any","note":"Blocks spoofed packets claiming to be from our own internal range"},{"cmd":"R2(config-ext-nacl)# permit tcp any host 203.0.113.50 eq 443","note":"Allows inbound HTTPS to the static-NAT'd file server from build 29"},{"cmd":"R2(config-ext-nacl)# permit tcp any any established","note":"Allows return traffic for connections R2's own hosts initiated"},{"cmd":"R2(config-ext-nacl)# deny ip any any log","note":"Denies and logs everything else arriving from the internet"},{"cmd":"R2(config-ext-nacl)# exit","note":"Returns to global configuration mode"},{"cmd":"R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet 0/2","note":"Selects R2's public WAN interface"},{"cmd":"R2(config-if)# ip access-group WAN-EDGE-IN in","note":"Applies the ACL inbound, filtering traffic arriving from the internet"},{"cmd":"R2(config-if)# end","note":"Returns to privileged EXEC mode"}],"notes":["The anti-spoofing deny at the top blocks any inbound packet falsely claiming to originate from our own 10.10.0.0/16 address space — that traffic should never legitimately arrive from the internet.","'established' matches only TCP packets that are part of an existing session, letting outbound-initiated connections receive their replies without opening the whole network to unsolicited inbound traffic."],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: this ACL permits exactly the traffic the branch needs from the internet — HTTPS to the one public-facing server, and replies to connections branch hosts themselves started — while blocking everything else including obviously spoofed traffic, right at R2's WAN edge. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: omitting the 'established' permit line would block all return traffic for outbound connections initiated by branch hosts, breaking ordinary web browsing and other client-initiated traffic entirely."},{"id":37,"title":"Full-topology build 37: GRE tunnel between R1 and R2","level":"INTER","cat":"Tunnels","purpose":"Create a stable virtual link between HQ and branch that can carry routing protocol traffic.","config":["enable","configure terminal","interface tunnel 0","ip address 172.16.1.1 255.255.255.252","tunnel source gigabitethernet 0/0","tunnel destination 192.168.12.2","end","configure terminal","interface tunnel 0","ip address 172.16.1.2 255.255.255.252","tunnel source gigabitethernet 0/0","tunnel destination 192.168.12.1","end","ping 172.16.1.2"],"steps":[{"cmd":"R1> enable","note":"Moves from user EXEC mode into privileged EXEC mode"},{"cmd":"R1# configure terminal","note":"Moves from privileged EXEC mode into global configuration mode"},{"cmd":"R1(config)# interface tunnel 0","note":"Creates a GRE tunnel interface on R1"},{"cmd":"R1(config-if)# ip address 172.16.1.1 255.255.255.252","note":"Assigns R1's side of the tunnel's own private addressing"},{"cmd":"R1(config-if)# tunnel source gigabitethernet 0/0","note":"Sources the tunnel from R1's existing WAN interface"},{"cmd":"R1(config-if)# tunnel destination 192.168.12.2","note":"Points the tunnel at R2's WAN address from build 22"},{"cmd":"R1(config-if)# end","note":"Returns to privileged EXEC mode"},{"cmd":"! On R2 (the matching tunnel endpoint):","note":"The corresponding tunnel configuration on the branch router"},{"cmd":"R2> enable","note":"Moves from user EXEC mode into privileged EXEC mode"},{"cmd":"R2# configure terminal","note":"Moves from privileged EXEC mode into global configuration mode"},{"cmd":"R2(config)# interface tunnel 0","note":"Creates the matching GRE tunnel interface on R2"},{"cmd":"R2(config-if)# ip address 172.16.1.2 255.255.255.252","note":"Assigns R2's side of the tunnel"},{"cmd":"R2(config-if)# tunnel source gigabitethernet 0/0","note":"Sources the tunnel from R2's WAN interface"},{"cmd":"R2(config-if)# tunnel destination 192.168.12.1","note":"Points the tunnel at R1's WAN address"},{"cmd":"R2(config-if)# end","note":"Returns to privileged EXEC mode"},{"cmd":"R1# ping 172.16.1.2","note":"Confirms the tunnel itself is up and passing traffic"}],"notes":["GRE alone (as configured here) provides no encryption — a production site-to-site design would typically add IPsec on top for confidentiality.","The tunnel's own 172.16.1.0/30 addressing is separate from every subnet already used elsewhere in this topology."],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: GRE encapsulates any Layer-3 protocol inside an IP packet between the tunnel's source and destination, creating a stable virtual point-to-point link over the existing WAN connection — useful for carrying traffic (like a routing protocol) that needs a consistent logical path regardless of the underlying network. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: if the underlay (the existing 192.168.12.0/30 WAN link) has no route between R1 and R2's tunnel-source addresses, the tunnel's line-protocol stays down even though the interface itself is administratively up."},{"id":38,"title":"HQ build 38: IPv6 ACL on R1","level":"INTER","cat":"Security","purpose":"Apply the same kind of traffic filtering to IPv6 as already exists for IPv4.","config":["enable","configure terminal","ipv6 access-list V6-MGMT-ONLY","permit tcp 2001:db8:acad:99::/64 any eq 22","permit icmp any any","deny tcp any any eq 23","permit ipv6 any any","exit","interface gigabitethernet 0/1","ipv6 traffic-filter V6-MGMT-ONLY in","end"],"steps":[{"cmd":"R1> enable","note":"Moves from user EXEC mode into privileged EXEC mode"},{"cmd":"R1# configure terminal","note":"Moves from privileged EXEC mode into global configuration mode"},{"cmd":"R1(config)# ipv6 access-list V6-MGMT-ONLY","note":"Begins a named IPv6 ACL"},{"cmd":"R1(config-ipv6-acl)# permit tcp 2001:db8:acad:99::/64 any eq 22","note":"Allows SSH only from the IPv6 MGMT prefix"},{"cmd":"R1(config-ipv6-acl)# permit icmp any any","note":"Explicitly permits ICMPv6, including neighbor discovery"},{"cmd":"R1(config-ipv6-acl)# deny tcp any any eq 23","note":"Blocks Telnet entirely, on any source"},{"cmd":"R1(config-ipv6-acl)# permit ipv6 any any","note":"Permits all other IPv6 traffic not otherwise matched"},{"cmd":"R1(config-ipv6-acl)# exit","note":"Returns to global configuration mode"},{"cmd":"R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet 0/1","note":"Selects the interface where the ACL will be applied"},{"cmd":"R1(config-if)# ipv6 traffic-filter V6-MGMT-ONLY in","note":"Applies the IPv6 ACL inbound"},{"cmd":"R1(config-if)# end","note":"Returns to privileged EXEC mode"}],"notes":["Unlike IPv4 ACLs, IPv6 ACLs have implicit permit rules for neighbor discovery — but adding an explicit 'permit icmp any any' here makes that intent visible rather than relying on the implicit behavior alone.","An explicit 'deny ipv6 any any' at the end (not used here) can accidentally break neighbor discovery if it isn't preceded by explicit ICMP permits — this ACL avoids that trap by ending with a broad permit instead."],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: this ACL mirrors the IPv4 security posture already established for R1 — SSH restricted to the management prefix, Telnet blocked outright — while explicitly preserving ICMPv6 neighbor discovery so the IPv6 link itself continues to function correctly. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: IPv6 ACLs use a similar top-down, first-match structure to IPv4 extended ACLs — placing the broad final permit ABOVE the specific deny/permit lines would make those specific rules unreachable."},{"id":39,"title":"Branch build 39: WLC AP-join prerequisites for the branch","level":"CORE","cat":"Wireless","purpose":"Prepare the branch network so a wireless access point can find and join its controller.","config":["enable","configure terminal","ip dhcp pool BRANCH-AP-POOL","network 10.10.40.0 255.255.255.0","default-router 10.10.40.1","option 43 hex f104.0a0a.c763","exit","ip domain-name acme.local","end","show wireless summary"],"steps":[{"cmd":"R2> enable","note":"Moves from user EXEC mode into privileged EXEC mode"},{"cmd":"R2# configure terminal","note":"Moves from privileged EXEC mode into global configuration mode"},{"cmd":"R2(config)# ip dhcp pool BRANCH-AP-POOL","note":"Creates a DHCP pool that will serve the branch's wireless access points"},{"cmd":"R2(dhcp-config)# network 10.10.40.0 255.255.255.0","note":"Serves addresses from the existing branch LAN subnet"},{"cmd":"R2(dhcp-config)# default-router 10.10.40.1","note":"Points APs at R2 as their gateway"},{"cmd":"R2(dhcp-config)# option 43 hex f104.0a0a.c763","note":"Encodes the WLC's management IP so APs can discover it automatically"},{"cmd":"R2(dhcp-config)# exit","note":"Returns to global configuration mode"},{"cmd":"R2(config)# ip domain-name acme.local","note":"Sets a domain name, also usable for DNS-based WLC discovery as an alternative to option 43"},{"cmd":"R2(config)# end","note":"Returns to privileged EXEC mode"},{"cmd":"R2# show wireless summary","note":"On a wireless-capable platform, confirms AP join status once an access point powers on"}],"notes":["Option 43's hex payload encodes the WLC's management IP address — a wrong encoding means the AP never finds the controller and stays stuck in Discovery mode.","10.10.40.0/24 is the same branch LAN subnet established in build 23, now also serving the branch's wireless access points."],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: lightweight access points discover their controller via DHCP option 43 (or a matching DNS record); providing that option in the branch's existing DHCP pool means a new AP plugged into the branch LAN can find and join the WLC automatically with no manual configuration. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: a wrong option-43 hex string (bad type/length/value encoding) means the AP never finds the controller and stays stuck in Discovery, even though basic IP connectivity and DHCP itself are working fine."},{"id":40,"title":"Branch build 40: WLAN SSID and security profile","level":"CORE","cat":"Wireless","purpose":"Broadcast a secured wireless network for branch employees once the AP has joined.","config":["enable","configure terminal","wlan BRANCH-WIFI 1 BRANCH-WIFI","security wpa akm dot1x","security dot1x authentication-list default","client vlan 40","no shutdown","end","show wlan summary"],"steps":[{"cmd":"(WLC) enable","note":"Moves the WLC CLI session into privileged EXEC mode"},{"cmd":"(WLC) configure terminal","note":"Moves into global configuration mode on the WLC"},{"cmd":"(WLC) wlan BRANCH-WIFI 1 BRANCH-WIFI","note":"Creates a WLAN profile with SSID 'BRANCH-WIFI'"},{"cmd":"(WLC config-wlan)# security wpa akm dot1x","note":"Selects 802.1X (RADIUS-backed) authentication instead of a pre-shared key"},{"cmd":"(WLC config-wlan)# security dot1x authentication-list default","note":"Ties the WLAN to the default authentication method list"},{"cmd":"(WLC config-wlan)# client vlan 40","note":"Places wireless clients onto the branch LAN VLAN established in build 23"},{"cmd":"(WLC config-wlan)# no shutdown","note":"Enables the WLAN so the SSID actually broadcasts"},{"cmd":"(WLC config-wlan)# end","note":"Returns to privileged EXEC mode"},{"cmd":"(WLC) show wlan summary","note":"Confirms the WLAN is enabled and reports its assigned VLAN"}],"notes":["Forgetting 'no shutdown' on the WLAN leaves the SSID fully configured but not actually broadcast to clients.","Placing wireless clients on VLAN 40 (the same branch LAN subnet used by wired branch hosts) keeps addressing consistent across wired and wireless access at the branch."],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: tying the WLAN to 802.1X authentication means each wireless user authenticates with their own credentials against a RADIUS server rather than a shared pre-shared key, and placing clients on VLAN 40 means they get addresses from the same DHCP pool and gateway (10.10.40.1) already serving wired branch hosts. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: leaving the WLAN in the default shutdown state after configuring everything else means it looks fully configured in 'show wlan summary' but never actually appears as an available network to nearby devices."},{"id":41,"title":"HQ build 41: VTP transparent mode and DTP nonegotiate on SW1","level":"CORE","cat":"Switching","purpose":"Protect the HQ VLAN database from an accidental overwrite via VTP.","config":["enable","configure terminal","vtp mode transparent","vtp domain ACME-HQ","end","show vtp status","configure terminal","vtp mode transparent","end"],"steps":[{"cmd":"SW1> enable","note":"Moves from user EXEC mode into privileged EXEC mode"},{"cmd":"SW1# configure terminal","note":"Moves from privileged EXEC mode into global configuration mode"},{"cmd":"SW1(config)# vtp mode transparent","note":"Keeps SW1 out of VLAN synchronization — it neither advertises nor accepts VTP updates"},{"cmd":"SW1(config)# vtp domain ACME-HQ","note":"Documents an administrative domain name even though transparent mode won't propagate VLANs via it"},{"cmd":"SW1(config)# end","note":"Returns to privileged EXEC mode"},{"cmd":"SW1# show vtp status","note":"Confirms transparent mode and the current VLAN database revision"},{"cmd":"! Repeated identically on SW2:","note":"The same protective setting applies to the second HQ switch"},{"cmd":"SW2> enable","note":"Moves from user EXEC mode into privileged EXEC mode"},{"cmd":"SW2# configure terminal","note":"Moves from privileged EXEC mode into global configuration mode"},{"cmd":"SW2(config)# vtp mode transparent","note":"Matches SW1's VTP mode"},{"cmd":"SW2(config)# end","note":"Returns to privileged EXEC mode"}],"notes":["VTP server/client mode has a well-known failure mode where a switch with a HIGHER VTP revision number — even a wiped lab switch — can silently overwrite an entire production VLAN database.","Transparent mode avoids that risk entirely, which is why both HQ switches in this topology use it deliberately rather than server/client mode."],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: transparent mode means SW1 and SW2 each maintain and control their own VLAN database locally, with no risk of one switch's VLANs (SALES, ENG, VOICE, MGMT, all carefully built up over this whole topology) being silently overwritten by a VTP update from an unexpected source. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: leaving either switch in VTP server or client mode means a third switch plugged in later — even accidentally, with a higher revision number from a previous lab — could wipe out the carefully-built VLAN database configured throughout this topology."},{"id":42,"title":"HQ build 42: root guard and loop guard on SW1's uplinks","level":"INTER","cat":"Switching","purpose":"Add STP protections appropriate for the trunk and transit links already built.","config":["enable","configure terminal","interface port-channel 1","spanning-tree guard loop","exit","interface gigabitethernet 1/0/25","spanning-tree guard root","end","show spanning-tree inconsistentports"],"steps":[{"cmd":"SW1> enable","note":"Moves from user EXEC mode into privileged EXEC mode"},{"cmd":"SW1# configure terminal","note":"Moves from privileged EXEC mode into global configuration mode"},{"cmd":"SW1(config)# interface port-channel 1","note":"Selects the SW1-SW2 EtherChannel bundle from build 12"},{"cmd":"SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree guard loop","note":"Protects this point-to-point inter-switch link against a unidirectional-link-induced loop"},{"cmd":"SW1(config-if)# exit","note":"Returns to global configuration mode"},{"cmd":"SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet 1/0/25","note":"Selects the routed uplink toward R1 from build 17"},{"cmd":"SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree guard root","note":"Ensures no unexpected device claiming a better root ever displaces SW1's intended root status via this port"},{"cmd":"SW1(config-if)# end","note":"Returns to privileged EXEC mode"},{"cmd":"SW1# show spanning-tree inconsistentports","note":"Confirms whether any port is currently blocked by root guard or loop guard"}],"notes":["Loop guard belongs on point-to-point links between switches (like the SW1-SW2 EtherChannel) — it protects against a stopped BPDU stream being misread as 'the other end is gone, start forwarding'.","Root guard belongs on ports facing where a lesser device must never become root — since gi1/0/25 is a routed port (not a switchport), this is illustrative of the general principle rather than a literal STP-relevant port in this specific topology."],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: loop guard on the SW1-SW2 bundle prevents an accidental bridging loop if that link's BPDU stream stops without the physical link actually failing, while root guard keeps SW1's deliberately-configured root status (from build 11) from ever being displaced by an unexpected device claiming a better priority. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: applying root guard to the SW1-SW2 link instead of an access-facing or non-root-intended port could block the legitimate root election between SW1 and SW2 that build 11 specifically configured."},{"id":43,"title":"HQ build 43: NETCONF/RESTCONF enablement on R1","level":"ADV","cat":"Automation","purpose":"Open R1 up to model-driven automation tooling alongside its normal CLI management.","config":["enable","configure terminal","netconf-yang","restconf","ip http secure-server","end","show netconf-yang status"],"steps":[{"cmd":"R1> enable","note":"Moves from user EXEC mode into privileged EXEC mode"},{"cmd":"R1# configure terminal","note":"Moves from privileged EXEC mode into global configuration mode"},{"cmd":"R1(config)# netconf-yang","note":"Starts the YANG datastore infrastructure NETCONF and RESTCONF both depend on"},{"cmd":"R1(config)# restconf","note":"Layers a RESTful HTTP/JSON API on top of the same datastore"},{"cmd":"R1(config)# ip http secure-server","note":"Enables the HTTPS server RESTCONF listens on"},{"cmd":"R1(config)# end","note":"Returns to privileged EXEC mode"},{"cmd":"R1# show netconf-yang status","note":"Confirms the NETCONF (port 830) listener is running"}],"notes":["Without 'netconf-yang' enabled first, RESTCONF has no YANG models to expose and requests fail even if the HTTPS server is otherwise reachable.","R1's existing local users (netadmin, backupadmin) can also authenticate NETCONF/RESTCONF sessions, since both ride on the same underlying credential store."],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: 'netconf-yang' starts the YANG datastore infrastructure and NETCONF listener, and 'restconf' layers a RESTful API on the same models, letting automation tools (Ansible, pyATS, custom scripts) manage R1's configuration the same structured way whether they speak NETCONF or REST. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: enabling only 'restconf' without 'netconf-yang' first leaves no YANG models for RESTCONF to actually expose, so requests fail even though the HTTPS server itself responds."},{"id":44,"title":"HQ build 44: EEM applet on a syslog match at SW1","level":"ADV","cat":"Automation","purpose":"Automatically react and log details whenever the SW1-R1 uplink flaps.","config":["enable","configure terminal","event manager applet UPLINK-FLAP-ALERT","event syslog pattern \"UPDOWN: Interface GigabitEthernet1/0/25, changed state to down\"","action 1.0 syslog msg \"ALERT: HQ uplink to R1 went down\"","action 2.0 cli command \"enable\"","action 2.1 cli command \"show ip interface brief\"","end"],"steps":[{"cmd":"SW1> enable","note":"Moves from user EXEC mode into privileged EXEC mode"},{"cmd":"SW1# configure terminal","note":"Moves from privileged EXEC mode into global configuration mode"},{"cmd":"SW1(config)# event manager applet UPLINK-FLAP-ALERT","note":"Names a new EEM applet"},{"cmd":"SW1(config-applet)# event syslog pattern \"UPDOWN: Interface GigabitEthernet1/0/25, changed state to down\"","note":"Watches for the exact syslog message when the R1-facing uplink goes down"},{"cmd":"SW1(config-applet)# action 1.0 syslog msg \"ALERT: HQ uplink to R1 went down\"","note":"Logs a clear, custom alert message"},{"cmd":"SW1(config-applet)# action 2.0 cli command \"enable\"","note":"Enters privileged EXEC mode within the applet's own action sequence"},{"cmd":"SW1(config-applet)# action 2.1 cli command \"show ip interface brief\"","note":"Automatically captures interface state at the moment of the event"},{"cmd":"SW1(config-applet)# end","note":"Returns to privileged EXEC mode"}],"notes":["This applet watches specifically for gi1/0/25, the exact interface configured as the SW1-to-R1 routed uplink in build 17.","The pattern is regex-based and must match the syslog text exactly, including the precise interface name as IOS reports it."],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: EEM's syslog event detector runs a pattern match against real syslog output; the moment the specific SW1-to-R1 uplink goes down, the numbered actions run in order — logging a clear custom alert and automatically capturing interface state for later troubleshooting, without anyone needing to be watching the console at that exact moment. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: a typo'd interface name or message format in the pattern means the applet silently never fires, since EEM's syslog matching requires an exact (regex) match against the real message text."},{"id":45,"title":"Full-topology build 45: extended ping and traceroute from R1 to the branch","level":"CORE","cat":"Verification","purpose":"Confirm HQ-to-branch reachability the way real application traffic would actually route.","config":["enable","ping","Protocol [ip]:","Target IP address: 10.10.40.50","Repeat count [5]: 20","Source address or interface: 10.10.100.2","traceroute 10.10.40.50"],"steps":[{"cmd":"R1> enable","note":"Moves from user EXEC mode into privileged EXEC mode"},{"cmd":"R1# ping","note":"Starts extended ping mode instead of a simple one-line ping"},{"cmd":"Protocol [ip]:","note":"Confirms IP as the protocol being tested"},{"cmd":"Target IP address: 10.10.40.50","note":"Targets a specific host on the branch LAN"},{"cmd":"Repeat count [5]: 20","note":"Sends 20 echoes instead of the default 5, for a more reliable reachability signal"},{"cmd":"Source address or interface: 10.10.100.2","note":"Sources the ping from R1's HQ-facing address rather than whichever interface IOS would pick by default"},{"cmd":"R1# traceroute 10.10.40.50","note":"Shows the hop-by-hop path from R1 to the branch host"}],"notes":["Sourcing from 10.10.100.2 (R1's address on the SW1 transit link) tests reachability the way traffic actually originating from deep inside HQ would be routed, not just from whatever interface is closest to the branch.","By this point in the build, this traffic crosses the SW1-R1 link (build 17), R1-R2 WAN link (build 18/22), and lands on the branch LAN (build 23) — a genuine end-to-end path exercised for the first time in this walkthrough."],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: extended ping's explicit source address setting is essential for testing reachability the way a specific internal host's traffic would actually be routed, rather than however IOS happens to pick a source by default; traceroute then shows exactly which hops (SW1, R1, R2) the traffic takes to confirm the whole topology built across this set is actually working end to end. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: a plain, non-extended ping from R1's own console can succeed via whatever default source IOS picks even while the actual intended traffic path is broken — always match the source to the real traffic path being tested."},{"id":46,"title":"Full-topology build 46: interpreting CDP/LLDP neighbors across the build","level":"CORE","cat":"Verification","purpose":"Confirm the physical topology matches what was actually intended and configured.","config":["enable","show cdp neighbors detail","show cdp neighbors gigabitethernet 1/0/25","configure terminal","lldp run","end","show lldp neighbors detail"],"steps":[{"cmd":"SW1> enable","note":"Moves from user EXEC mode into privileged EXEC mode"},{"cmd":"SW1# show cdp neighbors detail","note":"Lists every directly-connected Cisco device, including R1 and SW2, with their platform and IP"},{"cmd":"SW1# show cdp neighbors gigabitethernet 1/0/25","note":"Confirms specifically that R1 is seen on the expected uplink port"},{"cmd":"R1> enable","note":"Moves from user EXEC mode into privileged EXEC mode"},{"cmd":"R1# configure terminal","note":"Moves from privileged EXEC mode into global configuration mode"},{"cmd":"R1(config)# lldp run","note":"Enables the standards-based LLDP protocol on R1 as well, useful for any non-Cisco neighbor"},{"cmd":"R1(config)# end","note":"Returns to privileged EXEC mode"},{"cmd":"R1# show lldp neighbors detail","note":"Confirms LLDP-based neighbor discovery in addition to CDP"}],"notes":["CDP is Cisco-proprietary and works between SW1, SW2, R1, and R2 (all Cisco in this build); LLDP is the vendor-neutral standard, useful if a non-Cisco device is ever added.","Confirming neighbor detail here (platform, IP, local interface) is a fast way to catch a cabling mistake before it causes a confusing routing or spanning-tree problem later."],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: 'show cdp neighbors detail' confirms that SW1 is actually cabled to R1 (and SW2) exactly as the whole build assumed from the very first routed-uplink walkthrough — catching a wrong-port cabling mistake here is far faster than debugging a confusing routing symptom that traces back to it. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: some organizations disable CDP toward untrusted or external-facing edges to avoid leaking device information — a missing CDP neighbor doesn't always mean a cabling problem, it can also mean CDP itself was deliberately turned off on that specific link."},{"id":47,"title":"HQ build 47: diagnosing a duplex mismatch on SW1","level":"INTER","cat":"Verification","purpose":"Troubleshoot a subtle physical-layer problem using interface error counters.","config":["enable","configure terminal","show interfaces gigabitethernet 1/0/1 | include duplex","show interfaces counters errors","interface gigabitethernet 1/0/1","duplex auto","speed auto","end","show interfaces gigabitethernet 1/0/1 | include duplex"],"steps":[{"cmd":"SW1> enable","note":"Moves from user EXEC mode into privileged EXEC mode"},{"cmd":"SW1# configure terminal","note":"Moves from privileged EXEC mode into global configuration mode"},{"cmd":"SW1# show interfaces gigabitethernet 1/0/1 | include duplex","note":"Checks the current negotiated duplex on the Sales PC port from build 8"},{"cmd":"SW1# show interfaces counters errors","note":"Isolates just the error columns across every interface to spot a problem quickly"},{"cmd":"SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet 1/0/1","note":"Selects the affected port to correct the mismatch"},{"cmd":"SW1(config-if)# duplex auto","note":"Returns the port to auto-negotiation instead of a hard-set mismatched value"},{"cmd":"SW1(config-if)# speed auto","note":"Returns speed to auto-negotiation as well, so both sides negotiate together correctly"},{"cmd":"SW1(config-if)# end","note":"Returns to privileged EXEC mode"},{"cmd":"SW1# show interfaces gigabitethernet 1/0/1 | include duplex","note":"Confirms the corrected, matching duplex setting"}],"notes":["A high collision count on a modern switched network almost always means an unexpected duplex mismatch, since true collisions shouldn't happen at all on full-duplex links.","Hard-setting speed/duplex on only one side of a link (leaving the other on auto) is a classic cause of this exact mismatch."],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: comparing the negotiated duplex against the error counters quickly confirms whether late collisions and poor throughput on gi1/0/1 trace back to a duplex mismatch, and returning both speed and duplex to 'auto' on both ends of the link lets them correctly renegotiate matching settings together. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: hard-coding duplex to 'full' on just this one side without also checking (and correcting, if needed) the connected device's own setting can leave the mismatch in place even after this change, since duplex must match on BOTH ends of the link."},{"id":48,"title":"Branch build 48: password recovery concept on R2","level":"ADV","cat":"Device Basics","purpose":"Understand how to regain access to the branch router if its password is ever lost.","config":["confreg 0x2142","reset","configure terminal","config-register 0x2102","end","copy startup-config running-config","configure terminal","enable secret NewSecureP@ss2026","end","copy running-config startup-config"],"steps":[{"cmd":"! From ROMMON (device powered on with the console cable connected):","note":"This procedure requires physical console access to R2"},{"cmd":"confreg 0x2142","note":"Tells IOS to boot while ignoring startup-config, skipping the password prompt entirely"},{"cmd":"reset","note":"Reboots R2 with the new configuration register value"},{"cmd":"! After boot (startup-config was skipped, so no password is required):","note":"R2 now boots into a passwordless enable prompt"},{"cmd":"R2# configure terminal","note":"Enters global configuration mode"},{"cmd":"R2(config)# config-register 0x2102","note":"Resets the register back to normal boot behavior"},{"cmd":"R2(config)# end","note":"Returns to privileged EXEC mode"},{"cmd":"R2# copy startup-config running-config","note":"Reloads the ORIGINAL saved configuration (now visible) as the running configuration"},{"cmd":"R2# configure terminal","note":"Re-enters configuration mode to actually set a new, known password"},{"cmd":"R2(config)# enable secret NewSecureP@ss2026","note":"Sets a new enable secret, since the old one is presumed lost"},{"cmd":"R2(config)# end","note":"Returns to privileged EXEC mode"},{"cmd":"R2# copy running-config startup-config","note":"Saves the corrected configuration and password change permanently"}],"notes":["This procedure requires physical/console access to R2 by design — it's exactly why physical security of console ports matters as much as any password configured in software.","Register 0x2102 is the normal, standard boot behavior; 0x2142 is the temporary password-recovery value used only during this procedure."],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: register 0x2142 causes R2 to boot while ignoring startup-config, granting passwordless enable access; reloading the ORIGINAL startup-config as running-config (rather than starting from blank) preserves the entire build's configuration while only the password itself needs to be reset and re-saved. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: forgetting to reset the register back to 0x2102 after recovery would leave R2 skipping its startup-config on every future reload, effectively discarding this entire topology's configuration on the next power cycle."},{"id":49,"title":"HQ build 49: factory reset and reload on SW2","level":"INTER","cat":"Device Basics","purpose":"Understand what a full factory reset actually does before deciding to use one.","config":["enable","show running-config | include hostname","write erase","delete /force vlan.dat","reload","Proceed with reload? [confirm]"],"steps":[{"cmd":"SW2> enable","note":"Moves from user EXEC mode into privileged EXEC mode"},{"cmd":"SW2# show running-config | include hostname","note":"Confirms SW2's identity before proceeding with a destructive operation"},{"cmd":"SW2# write erase","note":"Deletes the saved startup configuration in NVRAM"},{"cmd":"SW2# delete /force vlan.dat","note":"Also removes the separate VLAN database file some platforms store outside the main config"},{"cmd":"SW2# reload","note":"Reboots the switch"},{"cmd":"Proceed with reload? [confirm]","note":"Confirms the reload — SW2 will come up in the initial setup dialog with no VLANs, no HSRP, none of this build's configuration"}],"notes":["'write erase' does NOT touch the currently running configuration — if the reload were cancelled at this point, SW2 would keep working exactly as before with the old config still active in RAM.","This procedure is shown here for understanding, not as a recommendation to actually erase SW2 — doing so would remove its entire role in this topology (VLANs, HSRP standby, EtherChannel membership) built up across every earlier walkthrough."],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: 'write erase' plus 'delete vlan.dat' plus 'reload' together return a switch to a genuinely blank factory state, useful when decommissioning hardware or handing it off for a completely different purpose — but exactly for that reason it should never be run on a device still serving a live role, like SW2's HSRP standby duties in this build. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: forgetting 'delete vlan.dat' on platforms that store VLAN information separately from the main configuration means old VLANs can persist even after a 'write erase' and reload, surprising anyone expecting a truly blank slate."},{"id":50,"title":"Capstone build 50: full end-to-end verification of the whole topology","level":"CORE","cat":"Verification","purpose":"Confirm every See \'git --help\'.'), ldiag('\u21b3 Common: init, clone, add, commit, status, branch, checkout, merge, push, pull, stash, log.') ]; } if(sub==='init'){ this.gitRepo=true; this.lastStatus=0; return [ lout('Initialized empty Git repository in '+this.cwd+'/.git/') ]; } if(sub==='clone'){ this.gitRepo=true; this.lastStatus=0; return [ lout('Cloning into \''+((a[1]||'repo').split('/').pop().replace(/\.git$/,''))+'\'...'), lout('done.') ]; } if(!this.gitRepo && ['add','commit','status','log','branch','checkout','switch','merge','push','pull','stash','diff','reset','rm','tag','fetch','rebase','restore'].indexOf(sub)>=0){ this.lastStatus=128; return [ lerr('fatal: not a git repository (or any of the parent directories): .git'), ldiag('\u21b3 Run "git init" here first, or "cd" into an existing repository.') ]; } if(sub==='add'){ if(!a[1]){ this.lastStatus=1; return [ lerr('Nothing specified, nothing added.'), ldiag('\u21b3 Stage files: "git add file" or "git add ." for everything.') ]; } this.gitStaged.push(a[1]); this.lastStatus=0; return []; } if(sub==='commit'){ if(a.indexOf('-m')<0){ this.lastStatus=0; return [ linfo('(opens editor for commit message)'), ldiag('\u21b3 Faster: "git commit -m \"message\"".') ]; } if(!this.gitStaged.length){ this.lastStatus=1; return [ lout('nothing to commit, working tree clean'), ldiag('\u21b3 Stage changes with "git add" before committing.') ]; } this.gitCommits++; this.gitStaged=[]; this.lastStatus=0; return [ lout('[main '+(this.gitCommits)+'] '+(a[a.indexOf('-m')+1]||'commit')), lout(' 1 file changed') ]; } if(sub==='status'){ this.lastStatus=0; return [ lout('On branch '+this.gitBranch), lout(this.gitStaged.length?'Changes to be committed:':'nothing to commit, working tree clean') ]; } if(sub==='log'){ this.lastStatus=0; return this.gitCommits? [ lout('commit a1b2c3 (HEAD -> '+this.gitBranch+')'), lout(' latest change') ] : [ lerr('fatal: your current branch \''+this.gitBranch+'\' does not have any commits yet') ]; } if(sub==='branch'){ if(a[1]){ this.lastStatus=0; return []; } this.lastStatus=0; return [ lout('* '+this.gitBranch) ]; } if(sub==='checkout'||sub==='switch'){ if(a.indexOf('-b')>=0||sub==='switch'&&a.indexOf('-c')>=0){ this.gitBranch=a[a.length-1]; } this.lastStatus=0; return [ lout('Switched to branch \''+(a[a.length-1]||this.gitBranch)+'\'') ]; } if(sub==='push'||sub==='pull'||sub==='fetch'){ this.lastStatus=0; return [ lout('Everything up-to-date') ]; } if(sub==='stash'){ this.lastStatus=0; return [ lout('Saved working directory and index state WIP on '+this.gitBranch) ]; } this.lastStatus=0; return []; }; LinuxShell.prototype.cAnsible = function(cmd,a){ if(cmd==='ansible-playbook'){ var f=a.filter(function(x){return x[0]!=='-';})[0]; if(!f){ this.lastStatus=1; return [ lerr('ERROR! You must specify a playbook file to run'), ldiag('\u21b3 e.g. "ansible-playbook -i inventory site.yml".') ]; } this.lastStatus=0; return [ lout('PLAY [all] ***'), lout('TASK [Gathering Facts] ***'), lout('PLAY RECAP *** ok=2 changed=1 failed=0') ]; } if(!a.length){ this.lastStatus=1; return [ lerr('usage: ansible [options]'), ldiag('\u21b3 e.g. "ansible all -m ping -i inventory".') ]; } this.lastStatus=0; return [ lout('host | SUCCESS => {"changed": false, "ping": "pong"}') ]; }; // expose (parity with ios_sim.js injection style) // (LinuxShell is referenced by the app IIFE after injection) window.LINUX_SAMPLES = [{"id":1,"title":"Inspect GRUB2 config","level":"CORE","cat":"System Management","purpose":"Locate and review the active GRUB2 configuration.","config":["ls /boot/grub2/","cat /boot/grub2/grub.cfg | head -30","grubby --default-kernel"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: GRUB2's runtime config is generated (not hand-edited) from /etc/default/grub and /etc/grub.d/ scripts via grub2-mkconfig, so grub.cfg reflects the current kernel list and boot options. `grubby --default-kernel` reports which kernel actually boots by default. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: editing grub.cfg directly works until the next `grub2-mkconfig` run silently overwrites your changes — always edit /etc/default/grub and regenerate."},{"id":2,"title":"Regenerate GRUB2 config","level":"CORE","cat":"System Management","purpose":"Persist a kernel parameter change into the boot loader.","config":["sudo vi /etc/default/grub","# add/edit: GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX=\"quiet net.ifnames=0\"","sudo grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX in /etc/default/grub supplies kernel boot parameters; `grub2-mkconfig` regenerates grub.cfg from that file plus the installed kernel list. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: on UEFI systems the output path differs (/boot/efi/EFI//grub.cfg) — writing to the BIOS path leaves the real config untouched and the change never takes effect."},{"id":3,"title":"Boot into rescue/emergency target","level":"INTER","cat":"System Management","purpose":"Force a single kernel parameter to drop into emergency mode for repair.","config":["# at the GRUB menu, press 'e' on the kernel line, then append:","systemd.unit=emergency.target","# press Ctrl-X / F10 to boot"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: appending systemd.unit=emergency.target (or rescue.target) at boot overrides the default target for that single boot, mounting root read-only with a minimal set of services — ideal for fixing fstab or password issues. WHY IT MATTERS: emergency.target skips even local-fs mounting beyond root, while rescue.target mounts local filesystems and starts more services; pick emergency for fstab repairs."},{"id":4,"title":"List and change systemd default target","level":"CORE","cat":"System Management","purpose":"Check and set the boot target (runlevel equivalent).","config":["systemctl get-default","sudo systemctl set-default multi-user.target","systemctl list-units --type=target"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: systemd targets replace SysV runlevels; `set-default` symlinks /etc/systemd/system/default.target to the chosen target so it's used on the next boot. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: setting default to graphical.target on a headless server with no display manager installed leaves the boot stuck waiting on a unit that can never start."},{"id":5,"title":"List loaded kernel modules","level":"CORE","cat":"System Management","purpose":"Show currently loaded modules and inspect one.","config":["lsmod | head","modinfo e1000e","lsmod | grep -i nvme"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: `lsmod` reads /proc/modules to list what's loaded right now; `modinfo` reads the module file itself for description, params and dependencies without loading it. WHY IT MATTERS: modinfo works even on modules that are NOT currently loaded, which is useful for checking compatibility before loading one."},{"id":6,"title":"Load, unload and persist a kernel module","level":"INTER","cat":"System Management","purpose":"Insert a module, remove it, and make it load at every boot.","config":["sudo modprobe nvme","lsmod | grep nvme","sudo modprobe -r nvme","echo nvme | sudo tee /etc/modules-load.d/nvme.conf"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: `modprobe` (unlike `insmod`) resolves and loads dependencies automatically from the module dependency database; writing the module name to /etc/modules-load.d/ tells systemd to load it at every boot. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: using `rmmod` instead of `modprobe -r` on a module that other modules depend on fails with 'in use' rather than cleanly unwinding the dependency chain."},{"id":7,"title":"Blacklist a kernel module","level":"INTER","cat":"System Management","purpose":"Prevent a problematic driver from auto-loading.","config":["echo \"blacklist nouveau\" | sudo tee /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist-nouveau.conf","sudo dracut --force # or: sudo update-initramfs -u","sudo reboot"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: a file under /etc/modprobe.d/ with `blacklist ` stops modprobe from auto-loading it via alias resolution; rebuilding the initramfs is required if the module is baked into early boot. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: blacklisting alone doesn't help if another module hard-depends on it, or if the module is already compiled into the initramfs image — you must regenerate initramfs and reboot."},{"id":8,"title":"Rebuild initramfs after driver change","level":"INTER","cat":"System Management","purpose":"Regenerate the initial RAM filesystem for the current kernel.","config":["sudo dracut -f /boot/initramfs-$(uname -r).img $(uname -r)","# Debian/Ubuntu equivalent:","sudo update-initramfs -u -k all"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: initramfs is a small filesystem loaded into RAM by the boot loader before the real root is mounted — it contains drivers/tools needed to find and mount root (e.g. LVM, RAID, NVMe, encryption). Changes to modules, LVM or /etc/crypttab require rebuilding it. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: forgetting to rebuild initramfs after adding a root-on-LVM or root-on-RAID module means the new kernel can boot but can't find/assemble the root device."},{"id":9,"title":"Identify the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard layout","level":"CORE","cat":"System Management","purpose":"Inspect key FHS directories and their purposes.","config":["ls -ld /etc /var /usr /opt /srv /tmp","df -h /var /usr","ls /var/log | head"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: the FHS defines fixed roles — /etc for host config, /var for variable runtime data (logs, spools, caches), /usr for shared read-only program files, /opt for third-party self-contained packages, /srv for served data. Following it lets any admin or tool predict where things live. WHY IT MATTERS: putting large log data on a small root partition (rather than a separate /var) is a classic cause of a filled-up root disk hanging the whole system."},{"id":10,"title":"List block devices and partitions","level":"CORE","cat":"System Management","purpose":"Enumerate disks, partitions, filesystems and mountpoints.","config":["lsblk -f","lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINT","cat /proc/partitions"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: `lsblk` reads sysfs to build a tree of block devices, partitions and their filesystem/mount info in one readable view — the modern replacement for parsing /proc/partitions by hand. WHY IT MATTERS: the -f flag adds filesystem type and UUID, which you need before writing /etc/fstab entries."},{"id":11,"title":"Partition a disk with fdisk (MBR)","level":"CORE","cat":"System Management","purpose":"Create a primary partition using the classic MBR tool.","config":["sudo fdisk /dev/sdb","# n (new), p (primary), accept defaults, w (write)","sudo partprobe /dev/sdb","lsblk /dev/sdb"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: fdisk edits the MBR partition table interactively; 'w' commits the change to disk, and `partprobe` tells the kernel to re-read the partition table without a reboot. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: forgetting to press 'w' means all your changes are discarded on quit — fdisk stages changes in memory until you explicitly write them."},{"id":12,"title":"Partition a disk with parted (GPT, scriptable)","level":"INTER","cat":"System Management","purpose":"Create a GPT label and partition non-interactively.","config":["sudo parted /dev/sdb mklabel gpt","sudo parted /dev/sdb mkpart primary ext4 1MiB 100%","sudo parted /dev/sdb print"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: parted supports GPT (needed for disks >2TiB or >4 primary partitions) and can be scripted non-interactively, unlike fdisk. Starting at 1MiB (not sector 0) aligns the partition to modern 4K-sector/SSD boundaries. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: using fdisk's MBR scheme on a disk larger than 2TiB silently caps usable capacity at 2TiB — GPT via parted or gdisk is required beyond that."},{"id":13,"title":"Partition a disk with gdisk (GPT, interactive)","level":"INTER","cat":"System Management","purpose":"Use the GPT-native equivalent of fdisk.","config":["sudo gdisk /dev/sdc","# o (new GPT), n (new partition), w (write)","sudo partprobe /dev/sdc"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: gdisk mirrors fdisk's interactive workflow but natively understands GPT structures (protective MBR, backup header at the end of the disk), which plain fdisk cannot safely edit. WHY IT MATTERS: GPT keeps a backup partition table at the end of the disk, so gdisk can often recover a corrupted primary table automatically."},{"id":14,"title":"Create and mount an ext4 filesystem","level":"CORE","cat":"System Management","purpose":"Format a new partition and mount it persistently.","config":["sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1","sudo mkdir -p /data","sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /data","blkid /dev/sdb1"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: `mkfs.ext4` writes filesystem metadata (superblock, inode tables, journal) onto the partition; `mount` attaches it into the directory tree at the mountpoint. `blkid` then reports the UUID needed for a durable fstab entry. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: mounting by device name (/dev/sdb1) in fstab instead of UUID breaks if disk enumeration order changes after adding/removing drives."},{"id":15,"title":"Add a persistent mount via /etc/fstab (UUID)","level":"CORE","cat":"System Management","purpose":"Make a filesystem mount automatically at boot using its UUID.","config":["blkid /dev/sdb1","sudo vi /etc/fstab","# UUID=1234-5678-ABCD /data ext4 defaults 0 2","sudo mount -a","findmnt /data"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: fstab fields are device, mountpoint, fstype, options, dump-flag, fsck-order; using UUID instead of a device path survives drive renumbering. `mount -a` tests every fstab entry without rebooting. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: a typo or missing device in fstab can drop the system into emergency mode at the next boot — always test with `mount -a` first, and consider the `nofail` option for non-critical mounts."},{"id":16,"title":"Create and activate a swap file","level":"CORE","cat":"System Management","purpose":"Add swap space without repartitioning.","config":["sudo fallocate -l 2G /swapfile","sudo chmod 600 /swapfile","sudo mkswap /swapfile","sudo swapon /swapfile","echo '/swapfile none swap sw 0 0' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: `fallocate` reserves the space, `mkswap` writes swap signature/metadata, and `swapon` activates it immediately; the fstab line makes it persistent across reboots. Restricting permissions to 600 prevents other users from reading process memory that gets paged out. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: skipping `chmod 600` leaves swap contents (which can include sensitive memory pages) world-readable on some filesystems."},{"id":17,"title":"Create an LVM physical volume and volume group","level":"INTER","cat":"System Management","purpose":"Prepare disks for LVM and pool them into a volume group.","config":["sudo pvcreate /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1","sudo vgcreate vg_data /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1","sudo vgs","sudo pvs"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: `pvcreate` writes LVM metadata onto each partition so it can be pooled; `vgcreate` combines physical volumes into one volume group, merging their space into a single allocatable pool. WHY IT MATTERS: LVM's power is that a volume group can span multiple physical disks, so a logical volume can grow beyond any single disk's size."},{"id":18,"title":"Create and grow a logical volume with a filesystem","level":"INTER","cat":"System Management","purpose":"Carve out a logical volume, format it, then extend it online.","config":["sudo lvcreate -L 20G -n lv_app vg_data","sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/vg_data/lv_app","sudo mount /dev/vg_data/lv_app /app","sudo lvextend -L +10G /dev/vg_data/lv_app","sudo resize2fs /dev/vg_data/lv_app"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: `lvcreate` allocates space from the VG into a logical volume; after growing it with `lvextend`, the filesystem itself must also be grown with a filesystem-specific tool (`resize2fs` for ext4, `xfs_growfs` for XFS) — extending the block device doesn't automatically resize the filesystem on top of it. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: running `lvextend` without following up with `resize2fs`/`xfs_growfs` leaves the extra space allocated but unusable — `df` still shows the old size."},{"id":19,"title":"Create a software RAID1 array with mdadm","level":"ADV","cat":"System Management","purpose":"Mirror two disks for redundancy using Linux software RAID.","config":["sudo mdadm --create /dev/md0 --level=1 --raid-devices=2 /dev/sdd1 /dev/sde1","cat /proc/mdstat","sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/md0","sudo mdadm --detail --scan | sudo tee -a /etc/mdadm.conf"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: mdadm assembles member partitions into a software RAID device that the kernel presents as one block device; --level=1 mirrors all writes to both members. Saving the array's UUID/layout to /etc/mdadm.conf lets it reassemble correctly and consistently across reboots. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: skipping the mdadm.conf step can cause devices to reassemble in a different, sometimes degraded order after reboot, especially with more than one array on the host."},{"id":20,"title":"Monitor and recover a degraded RAID array","level":"ADV","cat":"System Management","purpose":"Detect a failed RAID member and replace it.","config":["cat /proc/mdstat","sudo mdadm --detail /dev/md0","sudo mdadm /dev/md0 --remove /dev/sdd1","sudo mdadm /dev/md0 --add /dev/sdf1"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: /proc/mdstat and `mdadm --detail` show member state (active/faulty/spare); removing the faulty member and adding a replacement triggers an automatic resync onto the new disk while the array stays online (for RAID1/5/6/10). WHY IT MATTERS: RAID protects against a single disk failure, not against accidental deletion or corruption — it is not a backup strategy."},{"id":21,"title":"List PCI and USB hardware","level":"CORE","cat":"System Management","purpose":"Enumerate installed PCI devices and connected USB devices.","config":["lspci -k","lsusb -v | head -30","sudo dmidecode -t system"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: `lspci -k` shows PCI devices plus the kernel driver bound to each — useful for confirming a NIC or GPU has the right driver loaded. `dmidecode` reads SMBIOS/DMI tables for hardware inventory (vendor, model, serial) without opening the case. WHY IT MATTERS: lsusb needs root or udev rules to see full descriptor detail on some systems; running as a normal user may truncate output."},{"id":22,"title":"Basic KVM/QEMU VM creation concept","level":"ADV","cat":"System Management","purpose":"Verify virtualization support and create a VM disk + guest.","config":["egrep -c '(vmx|svm)' /proc/cpuinfo","lsmod | grep kvm","sudo qemu-img create -f qcow2 /var/lib/libvirt/images/vm1.qcow2 20G","sudo virt-install --name vm1 --memory 2048 --vcpus 2 --disk path=/var/lib/libvirt/images/vm1.qcow2 --cdrom /iso/install.iso --network network=default"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: a non-zero egrep count confirms hardware virtualization extensions (Intel VT-x/vmx or AMD-V/svm) are present and enabled in firmware; `qemu-img` allocates a copy-on-write-capable disk image, and `virt-install` scripts a full libvirt-managed VM definition. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: if /proc/cpuinfo shows 0, KVM acceleration is unavailable (often disabled in BIOS/hypervisor passthrough), and VMs will fall back to slow, full software emulation."},{"id":23,"title":"Core file management commands","level":"CORE","cat":"Services & User Management","purpose":"Copy, move, remove and link files safely.","config":["cp -a report.txt /backup/","mv draft.txt final.txt","rm -i old.log","ln -s /opt/app/app.conf /etc/app.conf","find /var/log -name '*.log' -mtime +30"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: `cp -a` preserves permissions/timestamps/links (archive mode); `ln -s` creates a symbolic link so one file can be referenced from multiple paths; `find -mtime +30` locates files older than 30 days for cleanup. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: using plain `rm *.log` in the wrong directory with no -i and no confirmation is a classic destructive mistake — always dry-run with `find ... -print` before piping to `-delete` or `xargs rm`."},{"id":24,"title":"Symbolic vs hard links","level":"CORE","cat":"Services & User Management","purpose":"Demonstrate the difference between symlinks and hard links.","config":["ln /data/file.txt /data/hardlink.txt","ln -s /data/file.txt /data/symlink.txt","ls -li /data/file.txt /data/hardlink.txt /data/symlink.txt"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: a hard link is a second directory entry pointing at the same inode (same data, same inode number, survives the original being deleted); a symlink is a separate inode holding a path string, which breaks if the target moves. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: hard links cannot cross filesystem/partition boundaries because inode numbers are only unique within one filesystem — attempting one gives 'Invalid cross-device link'."},{"id":25,"title":"Symbolic permission changes with chmod","level":"CORE","cat":"Services & User Management","purpose":"Grant execute to owner and remove group/other write access.","config":["chmod u+x deploy.sh","chmod go-w deploy.sh","ls -l deploy.sh"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: symbolic mode (u/g/o/a with +/-/=) adjusts specific permission bits relative to the current mode without needing to know the full octal value. WHY IT MATTERS: symbolic mode is safer for scripts that must not disturb unrelated bits, versus octal mode which always sets the exact absolute value."},{"id":26,"title":"Octal permission changes with chmod","level":"CORE","cat":"Services & User Management","purpose":"Set exact permission bits using octal notation.","config":["chmod 750 /srv/app/deploy.sh","chmod 644 /srv/app/config.yaml","stat -c '%A %a %n' /srv/app/deploy.sh"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: each octal digit sums read(4)+write(2)+execute(1) for owner/group/other respectively; 750 = rwxr-x---. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: `chmod 777` grants world write+execute on every file it touches — a common but serious security mistake that should almost never be used outside of throwaway lab scratch space."},{"id":27,"title":"Change ownership with chown and chgrp","level":"CORE","cat":"Services & User Management","purpose":"Transfer file ownership to another user and group.","config":["sudo chown deploy:webapps /srv/app -R","sudo chgrp webapps /srv/app/logs","ls -l /srv/app"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: `chown user:group` sets both owner and group in one call; `-R` recurses into subdirectories. Separating chgrp lets you change just the group without touching the owner. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: recursively chowning a directory that contains other users' files (e.g. a shared /tmp-like path) can break their access unexpectedly — scope -R carefully."},{"id":28,"title":"Set and verify umask","level":"CORE","cat":"Services & User Management","purpose":"Control default permissions for newly created files.","config":["umask","umask 027","touch newfile.txt","ls -l newfile.txt"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: umask is subtracted from the system default (666 for files, 777 for dirs) to compute default permissions for new files; 027 yields 640 for new files (rw-r-----). WHY IT MATTERS: umask set interactively in a shell doesn't persist — put it in /etc/profile, a user's shell rc file, or a systemd service's UMask= directive for it to apply consistently."},{"id":29,"title":"Set the setuid, setgid and sticky bits","level":"INTER","cat":"Services & User Management","purpose":"Use special permission bits for shared directories and privileged binaries.","config":["chmod g+s /srv/shared_project","chmod +t /srv/shared_project","ls -ld /srv/shared_project","ls -l /usr/bin/passwd"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: setgid on a directory makes new files inherit the directory's group (good for team-shared folders); the sticky bit on a directory (like /tmp) stops users deleting each other's files even with write access; setuid on a binary like /usr/bin/passwd lets it run with the file owner's (root) privileges to edit /etc/shadow. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: setuid on a directory has no meaning on Linux (only setgid and sticky do anything there) — a common exam-trap confusion."},{"id":30,"title":"Manage ACLs beyond the traditional permission model","level":"ADV","cat":"Services & User Management","purpose":"Grant a specific user extra access without changing group ownership.","config":["sudo setfacl -m u:jdoe:rwx /srv/app/data","getfacl /srv/app/data","sudo setfacl -x u:jdoe /srv/app/data"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: ACLs (Access Control Lists) let you assign fine-grained permissions to specific users/groups beyond the single owner/group/other model; the filesystem must be mounted with acl support (default on most modern ext4/xfs). WHY A VARIANT FAILS: forgetting that a plain `chmod` afterwards can collapse/mask ACL entries via the 'mask' entry — always re-check `getfacl` after any chmod on an ACL'd file."},{"id":31,"title":"Use chattr to make a file immutable","level":"ADV","cat":"Services & User Management","purpose":"Protect a critical file from modification or deletion, even by root.","config":["sudo chattr +i /etc/resolv.conf","lsattr /etc/resolv.conf","sudo chattr -i /etc/resolv.conf"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: the immutable attribute is enforced at the filesystem level, blocking writes, renames, and deletes for ALL users including root until the attribute is removed. WHY IT MATTERS: this is why editing a chattr +i file silently fails with 'Operation not permitted' even when run as root and even though normal permission bits look fine — always check `lsattr` when a permission error doesn't make sense."},{"id":32,"title":"Create users and groups","level":"CORE","cat":"Services & User Management","purpose":"Add a new user with a home directory and a supplementary group.","config":["sudo groupadd webapps","sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash -G webapps jdoe","sudo passwd jdoe","id jdoe"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: `useradd -m` creates the home directory from /etc/skel, -s sets the login shell, and -G adds supplementary (secondary) group membership; `passwd` sets the initial password since useradd alone leaves the account locked. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: forgetting -m leaves the user without a home directory, so their shell profile and default files never get created, and login may drop them at /."},{"id":33,"title":"Modify and delete user accounts","level":"CORE","cat":"Services & User Management","purpose":"Change a user's shell/group and later remove the account.","config":["sudo usermod -aG docker jdoe","sudo usermod -s /usr/sbin/nologin svc_app","sudo userdel -r jdoe"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: `usermod -aG` APPENDS a group without removing existing ones; `-G` alone would overwrite the whole supplementary group list. `userdel -r` removes the account plus its home directory and mail spool. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: using `usermod -G docker jdoe` instead of `-aG` silently wipes out every other supplementary group the user had — always use -aG when adding."},{"id":34,"title":"Inspect /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow and password aging","level":"INTER","cat":"Services & User Management","purpose":"Read account and password-aging metadata.","config":["getent passwd jdoe","sudo getent shadow jdoe","chage -l jdoe","sudo chage -M 90 -W 14 jdoe"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: /etc/passwd holds account metadata (UID/GID/home/shell) and is world-readable; /etc/shadow holds the actual hashed password and aging fields and is root-only. `chage -M 90 -W 14` enforces a 90-day max password age with a 14-day warning. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: directly editing /etc/shadow by hand risks corrupting the colon-delimited field layout — always use `chage`, `passwd`, or `vipw -s` which lock the file properly."},{"id":35,"title":"Query and manage package repos with dnf/yum","level":"CORE","cat":"Services & User Management","purpose":"Install, update and remove packages on RHEL-family systems.","config":["sudo dnf install -y httpd","sudo dnf update -y","dnf list installed | grep httpd","sudo dnf remove httpd"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: dnf resolves dependencies against configured repos and is the modern successor to yum on RHEL/Fedora/Alma/Rocky (yum is now an alias to dnf on most current releases). WHY IT MATTERS: `dnf update` upgrades all packages while `dnf update httpd` limits it to one — running blind full updates on a production box without testing is a common outage cause."},{"id":36,"title":"Query and manage packages with apt/dpkg","level":"CORE","cat":"Services & User Management","purpose":"Install, inspect and remove packages on Debian/Ubuntu.","config":["sudo apt update","sudo apt install -y nginx","dpkg -L nginx | head","sudo apt remove nginx"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: `apt` is the high-level, dependency-resolving front end; `dpkg` operates on individual .deb packages directly and can list installed files (-L) or query package details (-s) without touching the network. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: `dpkg -i package.deb` alone does NOT resolve missing dependencies — you'd need `apt install ./package.deb` or a follow-up `apt -f install` to fix broken deps."},{"id":37,"title":"Inspect an RPM package without installing it","level":"INTER","cat":"Services & User Management","purpose":"Query package metadata and file lists directly.","config":["rpm -qip package.rpm","rpm -qlp package.rpm","rpm -qa | grep kernel","rpm -V httpd"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: `rpm -q` queries the RPM database or a package file directly (info with -i, file list with -l) without needing dnf/yum or network access; `-V` verifies installed files against the package's recorded checksums/permissions, useful for detecting tampering. WHY IT MATTERS: rpm is the low-level tool dnf is built on — useful when dnf itself is broken or offline."},{"id":38,"title":"Install and manage snap/flatpak sandboxed apps","level":"INTER","cat":"Services & User Management","purpose":"Use universal packaging formats alongside the distro package manager.","config":["sudo snap install code --classic","snap list","flatpak install flathub org.videolan.VLC","flatpak list"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: snap and flatpak bundle an application with its own runtime/dependencies in a sandbox, so it installs/runs consistently across distros independent of the system package manager. WHY IT MATTERS: `--classic` on snap disables sandbox confinement for apps needing full system access (like editors with shell integration) — understand what you're opting out of before using it."},{"id":39,"title":"Manage a systemd service (start/enable/status)","level":"CORE","cat":"Services & User Management","purpose":"Control a service's running state and boot-time behavior.","config":["sudo systemctl start nginx","sudo systemctl enable nginx","systemctl status nginx","systemctl is-enabled nginx"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: `start`/`stop` affect the CURRENT running state only; `enable`/`disable` affect whether systemd creates the symlink to auto-start it at the NEXT boot — the two are independent. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: running only `enable` without `start` means the service won't run until the next reboot; assuming `enable` also starts it immediately is a common mix-up (use `enable --now` to do both)."},{"id":40,"title":"Reload a modified systemd unit file","level":"INTER","cat":"Services & User Management","purpose":"Apply changes to a custom unit and restart the service.","config":["sudo vi /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service","sudo systemctl daemon-reload","sudo systemctl restart myapp"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: systemd caches parsed unit files in memory; `daemon-reload` re-reads all unit files from disk so subsequent commands see the changes. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: editing a unit file and just running `restart` without `daemon-reload` first restarts the service using the OLD cached unit definition — a very common troubleshooting trap."},{"id":41,"title":"Read service logs with journalctl","level":"CORE","cat":"Services & User Management","purpose":"Filter systemd journal output for one service and follow it live.","config":["journalctl -u nginx --since today","journalctl -u nginx -f","journalctl -u nginx -p err --no-pager"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: `-u` filters to one systemd unit's log stream, `-f` follows new entries like `tail -f`, and `-p err` filters by minimum priority level (only error and worse). WHY IT MATTERS: journalctl output is binary-indexed and structured, so filtering by unit/priority/time is far more precise than grepping flat text log files."},{"id":42,"title":"Schedule recurring jobs with cron","level":"CORE","cat":"Services & User Management","purpose":"Add a per-user crontab entry to run a backup script nightly.","config":["crontab -e","# 30 2 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup.sh >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1","crontab -l"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: the five cron fields are minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week; `30 2 * * *` fires at 02:30 every day. Redirecting both stdout and stderr (2>&1) into a log file captures failures that would otherwise be silently discarded. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: cron jobs run with a minimal environment (no full PATH, no interactive shell profile) — scripts that work fine when run manually can fail under cron unless they use absolute paths or source the needed environment explicitly."},{"id":43,"title":"Schedule a one-time job with at","level":"INTER","cat":"Services & User Management","purpose":"Run a single deferred command at a specific future time.","config":["echo \"/usr/local/bin/report.sh\" | at 23:00","atq","atrm 3"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: `at` queues a one-off job for a specific time (unlike cron's recurring schedule); `atq` lists pending jobs and `atrm` cancels one by job number. WHY IT MATTERS: the atd daemon must be running for queued jobs to fire — on minimal installs it may need to be installed and enabled separately from cron."},{"id":44,"title":"Monitor and control processes","level":"CORE","cat":"Services & User Management","purpose":"Inspect running processes and manage their priority/state.","config":["ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head","top -o %MEM","renice -n 10 -p 4821","kill -15 4821"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: `ps aux` snapshots all processes; sorting by -%cpu surfaces top consumers. `renice` adjusts scheduling priority (nice value) of a running process without restarting it. `kill -15` (SIGTERM) politely asks a process to exit, allowing cleanup. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: reaching straight for `kill -9` (SIGKILL) skips a process's own cleanup/shutdown logic — try SIGTERM first and only escalate to -9 if the process ignores it."},{"id":45,"title":"Manage background jobs in a shell session","level":"INTER","cat":"Services & User Management","purpose":"Suspend, resume and background a long-running command.","config":["sleep 300","# press Ctrl-Z to suspend","jobs","bg %1","fg %1","disown %1"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: Ctrl-Z sends SIGTSTP, suspending the foreground job; `bg` resumes it in the background, `fg` brings it back to the foreground, and `disown` detaches it from the shell so it survives even if the shell exits. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: closing the terminal on a backgrounded-but-not-disowned job usually sends it SIGHUP and kills it too — use `disown` or `nohup`/`setsid` for jobs that must outlive the session."},{"id":46,"title":"Run and manage containers with podman","level":"ADV","cat":"Services & User Management","purpose":"Pull an image, run a rootless container, and inspect it.","config":["podman pull docker.io/library/nginx:latest","podman run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx:latest","podman ps","podman logs web"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: podman is daemonless and rootless-capable, mapping container UIDs to unprivileged host UIDs via user namespaces, unlike Docker's traditional root-owned daemon model. `-p 8080:80` publishes container port 80 on host port 8080. WHY IT MATTERS: rootless podman containers below port 1024 on the host require extra capability grants since unprivileged users normally can't bind low ports — that's why 8080, not 80, is mapped here."},{"id":47,"title":"Build a container image from a Dockerfile","level":"ADV","cat":"Services & User Management","purpose":"Write a minimal Dockerfile and build/run it.","config":["cat > Dockerfile <<'EOF'\nFROM alpine:3.19\nRUN apk add --no-cache curl\nCOPY entrypoint.sh /entrypoint.sh\nRUN chmod +x /entrypoint.sh\nENTRYPOINT [\"/entrypoint.sh\"]\nEOF","podman build -t myapp:1.0 .","podman run --rm myapp:1.0"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: each Dockerfile instruction creates a new cached layer; ordering RUN/COPY so rarely-changing steps (installing packages) come before frequently-changing ones (application code) maximizes build-cache reuse on rebuilds. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: forgetting `chmod +x` on the entrypoint script inside the image (host permissions don't always survive COPY faithfully across build contexts) causes 'permission denied' at container start even though the file looks fine on the host."},{"id":48,"title":"Generate an SSH key pair and copy it to a server","level":"CORE","cat":"Security","purpose":"Set up passwordless key-based SSH authentication.","config":["ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C \"jdoe@workstation\"","ssh-copy-id jdoe@server01","ssh jdoe@server01"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: `ssh-keygen` creates a private/public key pair (ed25519 is modern, fast, and small); `ssh-copy-id` appends the public key to the remote ~/.ssh/authorized_keys over an initial password login, after which key-based auth works without a password. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: if ~/.ssh or authorized_keys on the server has group/world write permissions, sshd refuses to use the key at all as a security precaution — permissions must be 700 for ~/.ssh and 600 for authorized_keys."},{"id":49,"title":"Harden sshd_config","level":"INTER","cat":"Security","purpose":"Disable root login and password auth, restrict to key-based access.","config":["sudo vi /etc/ssh/sshd_config","# PermitRootLogin no","# PasswordAuthentication no","# AllowUsers jdoe admin","sudo sshd -t","sudo systemctl restart sshd"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: disabling root login and password auth forces attackers to need a valid private key rather than brute-forcing a password, and `AllowUsers` whitelists exactly who may connect. `sshd -t` syntax-checks the config before reloading. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: restarting sshd with a config typo can lock out ALL remote access instantly — always run `sshd -t` first, and keep an existing session open while testing a new one in parallel."},{"id":50,"title":"Restrict sudo privileges with visudo","level":"CORE","cat":"Security","purpose":"Grant a user limited passwordless sudo for specific commands only.","config":["sudo visudo","# jdoe ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx","sudo -l -U jdoe"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: `visudo` locks the sudoers file and validates syntax before saving, preventing a broken file from locking out all sudo access; scoping to one exact command path (not a wildcard) limits the blast radius of that grant. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: editing /etc/sudoers directly with a plain text editor risks a syntax error that breaks sudo for EVERYONE, with no visudo-style pre-save validation to catch it."},{"id":51,"title":"Create a drop-in sudoers rule for a group","level":"INTER","cat":"Security","purpose":"Grant an entire admin group sudo access via /etc/sudoers.d/.","config":["echo '%sysadmins ALL=(ALL) ALL' | sudo tee /etc/sudoers.d/sysadmins","sudo chmod 440 /etc/sudoers.d/sysadmins","sudo visudo -c"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: files in /etc/sudoers.d/ are included automatically and let you manage grants modularly instead of editing one monolithic file; permissions must be exactly 440 (owner/group read-only) or sudo will ignore the file for safety. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: leaving the new file world-writable or executable causes sudo to reject it outright with a 'ignoring insecure file mode' warning."},{"id":52,"title":"Configure firewalld zones and services","level":"CORE","cat":"Security","purpose":"Open a service port using the RHEL-family dynamic firewall manager.","config":["sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones","sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=https --permanent","sudo firewall-cmd --reload","sudo firewall-cmd --list-all"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: firewalld manages zones (trust levels) with named services mapped to ports; `--permanent` writes the rule to persistent config, but it only takes effect after `--reload` merges it into the running ruleset. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: adding a rule with `--permanent` and forgetting `--reload` (or adding one without `--permanent` expecting it to survive a reboot) is the most common firewalld mistake — remember they're two separate rule sets, runtime and permanent."},{"id":53,"title":"Configure ufw on Debian/Ubuntu","level":"CORE","cat":"Security","purpose":"Enable the uncomplicated firewall and allow SSH plus HTTP.","config":["sudo ufw default deny incoming","sudo ufw allow OpenSSH","sudo ufw allow 80/tcp","sudo ufw enable","sudo ufw status verbose"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: ufw is a friendly front end over iptables/nftables; setting a default-deny policy first and explicitly allowing SSH BEFORE enabling ufw prevents you from locking yourself out over a remote session. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: running `ufw enable` before allowing your own SSH port immediately cuts your remote session with no way back in except console/out-of-band access."},{"id":54,"title":"Write nftables rules directly","level":"ADV","cat":"Security","purpose":"Build a modern nftables ruleset with a base chain.","config":["sudo nft add table inet filter","sudo nft add chain inet filter input { type filter hook input priority 0 \\; policy drop \\; }","sudo nft add rule inet filter input ct state established,related accept","sudo nft add rule inet filter input tcp dport 22 accept","sudo nft list ruleset"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: nftables is the modern successor to iptables, using tables/chains/rules with a unified syntax for IPv4+IPv6; the stateful `ct state established,related accept` rule lets return traffic for connections you initiated back in, which is required once the default policy is drop. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: setting `policy drop` on the input chain before adding the established/related and SSH-allow rules cuts off your own remote session the instant the ruleset is applied."},{"id":55,"title":"Manage legacy iptables rules","level":"ADV","cat":"Security","purpose":"Add and persist a basic iptables allow/deny ruleset.","config":["sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT","sudo iptables -A INPUT -m state --state ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT","sudo iptables -P INPUT DROP","sudo iptables-save | sudo tee /etc/sysconfig/iptables"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: iptables rules are evaluated top-down per chain, and `-A` appends to the end; `iptables-save` dumps the in-memory ruleset to a file that can be restored at boot with `iptables-restore` or a distro's persistence service. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: iptables rules are NOT persistent by default — a reboot without saving/reloading them silently reverts to an open (or distro-default) ruleset, undoing your hardening."},{"id":56,"title":"Check and set SELinux enforcement mode","level":"INTER","cat":"Security","purpose":"Verify SELinux status and switch between modes.","config":["getenforce","sudo setenforce 0","sestatus","sudo vi /etc/selinux/config","# SELINUX=enforcing"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: `setenforce 0/1` toggles enforcing vs permissive at runtime (permissive logs denials but doesn't block them, useful for debugging); the persistent boot-time mode is set separately in /etc/selinux/config. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: setting SELinux to `disabled` (not just permissive) in the config requires relabeling the entire filesystem on next boot if you ever re-enable it, and disables SELinux's audit logging entirely in the meantime — permissive is almost always the better troubleshooting choice."},{"id":57,"title":"Fix an SELinux context / file labeling issue","level":"ADV","cat":"Security","purpose":"Diagnose and correct a mislabeled web content directory.","config":["ls -Z /var/www/html/index.html","sudo semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t '/srv/www(/.*)?'","sudo restorecon -Rv /srv/www"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: SELinux enforces policy based on file context labels (type), not just Unix permissions; `semanage fcontext` registers the correct label pattern for a non-standard content path, and `restorecon` actually applies it to existing files. WHY A VARIANT FAILS: moving web content to a custom directory outside /var/www without relabeling leaves files with the wrong context (often default_t), so Apache gets 'permission denied' even though normal chmod/chown looks completely correct — this is the single most common SELinux troubleshooting scenario."},{"id":58,"title":"Toggle an SELinux boolean","level":"ADV","cat":"Security","purpose":"Allow httpd to make outbound network connections via a policy boolean.","config":["getsebool httpd_can_network_connect","sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on","getsebool -a | grep httpd"],"explain":"WHY IT WORKS: booleans are pre-built policy toggles for common scenarios (like a web app needing outbound DB connections) without writing custom policy; `-P` makes the change persistent across reboots by rewriting the policy store, not just the in-memory state.
